title: Chapter 13 — Cooking: Wall Ovens, Microwaves & Compact Cooking
intro: The built-in cooking wall — wall ovens, speed ovens, microwave placement, and renovation selling.

sections.title: Wall Oven Fundamentals
sections.content:
Wall ovens come in three standard widths: 24, 27, and 30 inches. The width determines the cutout size — this is non-negotiable and must match the existing cabinet opening unless they are renovating.

Single versus double is the first question. Ask: 'How often do you cook for more than six people?' If rarely, a single wall oven with a speed oven or microwave above it often beats a double wall oven. The combination gives them more cooking versatility in less space.

Convection matters. True convection has a dedicated heating element around the fan — it bakes more evenly across all racks. Fan-assist convection just circulates the air from the main elements. At the premium tier and above, true convection is standard. At mid-range, it is the differentiator worth the step-up.

sections.title: The Microwave Evolution
sections.content:
Microwaves are being replaced in luxury and premium kitchens — not by nothing, but by speed ovens and built-in multi-function units that do microwave plus convection plus steam in a single cavity.

For mainstream customers, the over-the-range microwave is still the most common placement. It serves double duty as ventilation and cooking. But it is a compromise — the ventilation is weaker than a dedicated hood, and the microwave is at an awkward height for shorter users.

Microwave drawers are the premium alternative. They install below the counter at a comfortable height. Sharp and several others make them. They are excellent for accessibility and for freeing up wall space.

The countertop multi-function revolution is real. Three-in-one, four-in-one, and six-in-one countertop appliances are replacing the microwave for customers who want more cooking versatility without giving up counter space. Know what is on your floor.

sections.title: Speed Ovens and Combi-Steam
sections.content:
Speed ovens combine microwave energy with convection heating. They cook up to four times faster than a conventional oven while delivering convection-quality results. This is not a microwave that can bake — it is an oven that can also use microwave energy.

Combi-steam ovens combine steam with convection. They produce bakery-quality bread, perfectly moist proteins, and restaurant-level vegetables. Miele, Gaggenau, Wolf, Thermador, and Bosch Benchmark all offer them.

At the luxury tier, the cooking column — a stack of wall oven plus speed oven or combi-steam — is replacing the traditional double wall oven. It gives the customer more cooking modes in the same wall space.

The key question for the customer: 'Do you want speed, steam, or both?' Speed ovens are about convenience. Combi-steam is about culinary results. Some units do both.

sections.title: Selling the Cooking Wall
sections.content:
When a customer is renovating and choosing between a range and separates — cooktop plus wall oven — this is a design conversation as much as a product conversation.

Separates give design flexibility. The oven can be at an ergonomic height instead of bending to the floor. The cooktop can sit on an island. The hood can be a statement piece. This is a renovation or new-build conversation.

A range is simpler, more affordable, and one product to choose. For a standard kitchen replacement, the range is usually the right answer.

The customer who is considering separates is typically spending $8,000-$15,000 on cooking alone. They need the design consultation. They need installation coordination. They need someone who understands how all these pieces fit together — physically and visually.

This is where you earn the package sale. And this is where getting the installation requirements right prevents a $500 callback.
